newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian gas official found safe after kidnapping. [CORRECTED 1300 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian gas official found safe after kidnapping. [CORRECTED 1300 GMT]

text.p: A top official of Bulgaria's state gas firm has been freed by police after being kidnapped on the orders of a rival gas interest, the interior ministry said on Friday.

"Natural gas interests were at the base (of the kidnapping)," Prime Minister Ivan Kostov told reporters at an interior ministry conference, referring to the release of Bulgargas deputy head Penko Dimitrov, who was freed on Thursday night after being held for about 22 hours.
(Corrects to make clear the confrence was not called to announce the release).

"It was ordered by Vesselin Todorov, linked to a firm whose economic interests were badly hurt by the principled position of the Bulgargas management and personally by that of Penko Dimitrov," an interior ministry statement said.

The ministry said the kidnapping was carried out by the Elos private security firm, which recorded a call from Todorov ordering the kidnap and instructing them to break the Bulgargas executive's arms and legs and disable him for life.
Apparently hoping to get a higher price elsewhere, the head of Elos met Dimitrov and played him the tape. He then took him to a house in Sofia telling him he was protecting him.
"All the people who have ordered the kidnapping were arrested," Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev told reporters. He gave no more details.

The ministry said last month it had to provide protection for Bulgargas executive director Vassil Filipov after he received threats. But it said there was no link between the threats against Filipov and Dimitrov's kidnap.
On Tuesday, explosives planted in a road outside Sofia damaged two cars belonging to the powerful business conglomerate Multigroup, in an apparent attempt to assassinate its president, Ilia Pavlov.
But Pavlov was not in either of the cars when the attack took place.
Bulgaria's new government, which took office on May 21, has vowed to crack down on organised crime, which has boomed since the end of communist rule in 1989.

"There is one enemy now in our society and that is fear of organised crime...If we succeed in fighting fear in society it is sure that we will win the fight against corruption," Kostov told Friday's conference.
